items.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995
items.q: Earl Hines is home, in Philadelphia, with Janie his wife, and they had us over for dinner, the Basie band.

ctx.x: Yeah, he could sleep around us. I remember another wonderful afternoon. We used to play up in Philadelphia, we played Pep’s. And we’d start there by playing a Monday matinee. So you know we’d be off then for several hours before the evening performance would start at 8:30 or 9:00, 9:00 at night started the evening performance on Monday. So

Earl Hines is home, in Philadelphia, with Janie his wife, and they had us over for dinner, the Basie band. They had this long table set up man, with greens, corn bread and ham hocks and corn and all kinds of marvelous things. And I’ve forgotten what the dessert was, whether it was sweet potato pie or lemon cream pie or whether it was pie with strawberries, but it was a delicious looking thing. We’re sitting there eating, and here comes Basie standing around, you know Basie, he had a drink, he had some scotch, he…

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn’t have an opportunity to work too much with Gates, except on a couple of occasions with a small group

ctx.x: Earl Hines was a marvelous leader. I didn’t have an opportunity to work too much with Gates, except on a couple of occasions with a small group, after he had Marva [Josie], the singer, and Budd Johnson was with him at the time. But he was a nice man, a great musician. I’m very proud of the fact that he got Louis Armstrong involved in – with his playing, or Louis got him involved. They inspired each other. But
Louis played – Earl played what they call the trumpet-style on piano. He was a good musician.
